headline: High: Gemini CLI’s default filesystem, shell, git, and MCP access can conflict with a non-runnable content list only if manually bridged; leakage and compliance risks are limited by the pair’s asymmetry.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Agent A is a non-runnable content-writing list with no I/O surfaces, while agent B can read files, use MCP, and parse user-approved tool outputs. A direct injection path is not documented, so the only plausible bridge is manual copy/paste or user-created files, which keeps blast radius small.
conditions: IF the operator copies A-generated text into B prompts or files, B may follow injected instructions.
IF B is configured to ingest shared files from A without review, prompt injection becomes possible.
mitigations: Avoid copying A output into B prompts without sanitizing instructions.
Use a separate review step before B consumes any A-authored file.
Disable or restrict MCP servers for sessions that process untrusted text.
Keep A and B in separate directories to reduce accidental bridging.

B_data_leakage.rationale: A exposes no data classes and has no filesystem or network surfaces, while B touches source code, cwd files, and shell environment and can egress broadly. Because A itself is only a docs/list profile, the pairwise leakage path is limited unless the operator places sensitive files into B’s workspace.
conditions: IF sensitive files are placed in B's cwd, B can read and transmit them.
IF A is used as a source of copied content containing secrets, B may expose that content through its broad egress.
mitigations: Do not place secrets in B’s working directory.
Run B in a dedicated non-sensitive workspace.
Turn off network egress when processing confidential material.
Review any files before passing them from A to B.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: A has no write or concurrency surface, but B can write the filesystem, modify git state, and shares state via filesystem and git across instances. The pair does not show a direct conflict with A, yet B’s default mutable access creates a real overlap if A-derived artifacts are stored in the same workspace.
conditions: IF A-derived files are placed in the same git repo used by B, concurrent edits can collide.
IF multiple B instances operate on the same workspace, git and filesystem races can occur.
mitigations: Use one workspace per B session.
Commit or stash changes before starting another B instance.
Keep A artifacts outside the git repo until finalized.
Enable filesystem-level isolation such as separate directories.

D_cascading_error.rationale: A is a content list, not an action-taking agent, so B cannot automatically treat A’s output as authoritative unless the operator manually feeds it in. B does have tool use and shell authority, but the pair lacks a documented automated pipeline, making cascading error mainly a manual workflow risk.
conditions: IF the operator uses A output as source material for B without verification, B may propagate errors.
IF B is instructed to act on A-authored claims, downstream shell or git actions can amplify mistakes.
mitigations: Require human verification of A output before B acts on it.
Separate drafting from execution in the workflow.
Use checklists for any B action based on A content.
Log the provenance of A-derived claims before execution.

E_compliance.rationale: A is an open-source content list with no touched data classes, while B handles source code, cwd files, shell environment, and optional Google-account login plus API-key secrets. No residency or regulated-data mismatch is evidenced for the pair, so compliance risk is limited to ordinary handling of local code and secrets.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed into B's workspace or prompts, compliance obligations increase.
IF Google account login or API-key handling is enabled for sensitive environments, local policy review is required.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of B sessions.
Use least-privilege credentials for B.
Review retention settings before processing sensitive files.
Prefer local-only workflows for confidential code.
